questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a login and a user in SQL Server/Azure SQL?
options: A login is a server-level object that answers "can this identity connect at all"; a user is a database-level object that answers what it can do inside one specific database
Logins and users are two names for the exact same object
A user always grants more access than a login
Logins only exist in Azure SQL Database, never in Managed Instance
questions.explain: This is the core hierarchy: server-level logins control connection, database-level users control what happens inside a specific database once connected.

questions.q: Why can the same login map to users with different names and different permissions in different databases on the same server?
options: Because the user object is created separately per database with CREATE USER ... FOR LOGIN, so each database defines its own mapping and permissions independently
Because logins automatically get identical permissions everywhere
Because this is not actually possible in SQL Server
Because only Managed Instance supports multiple databases per server
questions.explain: Each database's CREATE USER FOR LOGIN statement independently decides the user's name and permissions in that database — the mapping isn't shared or forced to match across databases.

questions.q: Which of these is a fixed SERVER role, applying across the entire server rather than one database?
options: sysadmin
db_owner
db_datareader
db_datawriter
questions.explain: sysadmin is a fixed server role granting full control of the entire server; db_owner, db_datareader, and db_datawriter are fixed database roles scoped to a single database.

questions.q: What does the public role represent at both the server and database scope?
options: An automatic membership every login (server) or every user (database) gets, granting only minimal baseline rights
Full administrative control at that scope
A role that must be manually assigned to each login one at a time
A role that only exists in on-premises SQL Server, not Azure SQL
questions.explain: Every login is automatically in the server's public role, and every database user is automatically in the database's public role — both carry minimal baseline rights, not elevated access.

questions.q: Why does separating server-level logins from database-level users scale better than a single flat permission list?
options: It lets one login have completely different access in different databases on the same server, which matters when one server hosts production, reporting, and staging databases side by side
It removes the need for any permissions at all
It means every login automatically gets db_owner everywhere
It eliminates the need for fixed roles entirely
questions.explain: The two-level structure is exactly what allows the same identity to have very different, appropriately scoped access across multiple databases on one server.
